title: Cups: US, UK, Metric — Three Sizes
h1: The cup — a recipe unit with three different volumes
description: A US cup is 236.6 mL. A metric cup is 250 mL. A UK teacup is 284 mL. Here is why baking recipes cross international lines so badly.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against USDA and NIST Handbook 44

hero: 'One cup of flour' means three different weights of flour depending on which cup — and that is before we get into loose vs sifted.
body: The cup as a cooking measure was standardised in the US at 8 fl oz in the 1890s. Australia and New Zealand later chose 250 mL for round-number metric convenience. The UK never officially adopted a cup at all — traditional British recipes weigh ingredients instead. Modern recipe apps rarely make the distinction clear.

> US legal cup (nutrition labelling) = 240 mL
> US customary cup = 236.588 mL = 8 US fl oz
> Metric cup (Australia, NZ, Canada) = 250 mL
> UK breakfast cup (historic) = 284 mL = 10 UK fl oz
> Japanese cup (traditional) = 200 mL

1 US cup of all-purpose flour weighs 120 g if spooned lightly, 140 g if scooped, 160 g if scooped and tapped. That is a 33% spread from measurement technique alone, before any unit conversion. This is why serious baking recipes now list grams — the cup is a rough approximation, not a precise volume.

A US recipe calling for 3 cups of flour = 3 × 236.6 = 710 mL. Followed with a metric measuring cup (3 × 250 = 750 mL), you add 5.6% more flour — enough to make the cookies noticeably drier. Followed with a UK teacup (3 × 284 = 852 mL), you add 20% more flour and the recipe fails.

Liquid ingredients (water, milk, oil): volume is repeatable, and a 5% error is invisible in most dishes. Chopped vegetables, nuts, herbs: cups are a rough estimate anyway. Salt, spices: switch to teaspoons or grams — cup measurements are wildly inaccurate at small scales.
US cup = 237 mL. Metric cup = 250 mL. UK cup = 284 mL. For baking, weigh ingredients — cups are approximations.

faqs.q: Which cup is on US nutrition labels?
faqs.a: The 'US legal cup' = 240 mL, mandated by the FDA. It is 3.4 mL bigger than the traditional 236.6 mL cup.
Rarely. Traditional UK baking uses ounces and grams. Modern UK cookbooks influenced by US authors may use 250 mL metric cups.
US convention: 1/2 cup = 4 oz = 113 g. Butter sold outside the US does not come in sticks and this unit does not travel.
